TVET Curriculum · EV Manufacturing Automation Track

EV Automated Line Technician Program

A six‑module, digital‑twin‑anchored curriculum covering the four robotic stations of a modern EV assembly line — Body Assembly, Paint, General Assembly, and Quality Systems — built around one core outcome: technicians who can diagnose and respond to chronic bottlenecks, not just react to full line stops.

24 hrsTotal contact time
6Modules
4Digital twin lab stations
Foundation → DiagnosticProgression
EV / AutomotiveSector
M1

EV Automated Line Overview & Digital Twin Orientation

3 hrs ▸
Learning Objectives
  • Describe the four‑station flow of a modern EV body‑in‑white‑to‑shipment line and the role of automation at each stage.
  • Navigate the 5D digital twin: rotate/zoom the scene, read the live HMI strip, and interpret station status indicators.
  • Distinguish a sporadic line stop (sudden, visible, alarms trigger) from a chronic loss (small, recurring, often unalarmed) using OEE vocabulary.
Key Concepts

Line balancing and takt time · robotic vs. manual work content in EV assembly · the "digital twin" as a live data layer over the physical line · Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) = Availability × Performance × Quality.

Digital Twin Lab Activity
  1. Open the Simulator tab and step through all four stations using the station picker.
  2. Record baseline KPIs (cycle time, units/hr, OEE, reject rate) in the trainee logsheet.
  3. Let the line run for 2 minutes of simulated time; note any natural micro‑variation in cycle time — this is the first exposure to "normal noise" vs. a real bottleneck signal.
Assessment

Quiz (10 items, station sequence & OEE formula) + completed baseline logsheet.

M2

Station 1 — Body Assembly (BIW): Robotic Welding Systems

3.5 hrs ▸
Learning Objectives
  • Explain the body‑in‑white process: sheet metal framing, fixture clamping, and multi‑robot spot/arc welding sequences.
  • Identify the two most common chronic failure modes in robotic welding cells: electrode tip wear and TCP (tool‑center‑point) drift.
  • Read a weld‑quality trend chart and recognize gradual degradation before it becomes a full reject spike.
Technical Content
Sub‑systemFunctionCommon Chronic Issue
Framing fixture / jigHolds panels to tolerance during weldLocator pin wear → repeatable position drift
Spot‑weld robot & gunDelivers current + pressure at weld pointsElectrode tip mushrooming → resistance rise, weak nugget
Robot arm / controllerPositions gun at programmed TCPTCP drift after minor collision or servo wear
Material handling (skid/AGV)Indexes body between stationsChain pitch wear → mis‑index, part misalignment
Digital Twin Lab Activity

On the Simulator tab, select ST‑01 Body Assembly and run all four fault scenarios (Electrode Tip Wear, TCP Drift, Fixture Locator Pin Wear, and Weld Cable/Shunt Resistance Buildup). For each, complete the diagnostic worksheet before revealing the answer, then log the corrective action and estimated downtime‑per‑occurrence.

Assessment

Scenario diagnostic worksheet (all four faults) + short written response: "Why does electrode wear cause a chronic loss instead of a sudden stop?"

M3

Station 2 — Paint Process: Corrosion Protection & Coating Robotics

3.5 hrs ▸
Learning Objectives
  • Describe the paint sequence: e‑coat (cathodic dip) for corrosion protection, sealant application, basecoat, and clearcoat.
  • Explain how booth environment (temperature, humidity, air handling) and applicator condition (nozzle, bell cup) affect finish quality.
  • Connect a rising touch‑up/rework rate to specific upstream process drift rather than treating it as random.
Technical Content
Sub‑systemFunctionCommon Chronic Issue
E‑coat tankElectro‑deposits primer for corrosion resistanceBath contamination / voltage drift → thin coverage in recesses
Spray robot / bell applicatorApplies base & clear coatNozzle partial clog → uneven film build, orange‑peel defects
Booth climate controlMaintains cure conditionsHumidity/temperature drift → adhesion & gloss variance
Color‑change valve setSwitches color per mixed‑model sequenceValve seal wear → cross‑contamination between colors
Digital Twin Lab Activity

Select ST‑02 Paint and run all four scenarios (Spray Nozzle Partial Clog, Booth Humidity Drift, Bell Cup Bearing Wear, and E‑coat Bath Contamination Buildup). Trainees plot simulated defect rate over 20 simulated cycles to visualize a chronic (gradual) trend versus a sporadic (step‑change) trend.

Assessment

Diagnostic worksheet + trend‑chart classification exercise (chronic vs. sporadic).

M4

Station 3 — General Assembly & EV Powertrain/Battery Integration

4 hrs ▸
Learning Objectives
  • Describe the general assembly sequence for an EV: interior trim, wiring harness routing, and the battery‑pack & e‑motor "marriage" operation (underbody mating of the battery/drive unit to the body).
  • Identify torque‑critical and high‑voltage‑safety‑critical fastening points and why their failure modes are often silent.
  • Explain why torque‑tool degradation is a textbook "chronic, hard‑to‑detect" bottleneck.
Technical Content
Sub‑systemFunctionCommon Chronic Issue
Marriage station lift/AGVMates battery pack & drive unit to body underbodyFastener feeder jam → intermittent stoppage, not always alarmed
Servo / pneumatic torque toolsFastens HV battery mounts, structural jointsAir pressure drop or bit wear → progressive under‑torque
Wiring harness robot / cobotRoutes & clips HV and LV harnessesGripper wear → dropped clips, missed routing points
Parts sequencing (JIS/JIT feed)Delivers correct trim part in build sequenceSequencing software mismatch on mixed‑model runs
Note on the source footage

The reference walkthrough video shows a conventional engine/transmission assembly sequence. This module reframes the same station logic for an EV context — battery pack and e‑motor integration replace engine/transmission installation, but the automation, fastening, and diagnostic principles transfer directly.

Digital Twin Lab Activity

Select ST‑03 General Assembly and run all four scenarios (Torque Tool Air Pressure Drop, Battery Pack Fastener Feeder Jam, Harness Routing Gripper Wear, and Parts Sequencing (JIS) Mismatch). Trainees must decide which fault would not be caught until Station 4 — setting up Module 6's cascade lab.

Assessment

Diagnostic worksheet + HV safety checklist (identify which faults require lockout/tagout before intervention).

M5

Station 4 — Quality Systems & End‑of‑Line Testing

3.5 hrs ▸
Learning Objectives
  • Describe the three‑stage EOL check sequence: system check, parts/assembly verification, functional test.
  • Explain the role of machine vision and roll/functional test rigs in catching defects that earlier stations cannot self‑detect.
  • Recognize that Quality is the station where upstream chronic losses become visible — and why that makes root‑cause tracing harder, not easier.
Technical Content
Sub‑systemFunctionCommon Chronic Issue
Vision inspection camera arrayChecks part presence, gaps, surface defectsCamera/lighting calibration drift → false rejects or missed defects
EOL roll‑test rigRuns powertrain & braking functional testSensor noise → intermittent false‑fail, retest loops
HV insulation test stationVerifies battery/HV system safety before shipmentTest lead contact resistance drift → inconsistent readings
Traceability/MES linkLogs pass/fail and links back to build dataData‑logging gaps that hide the true upstream source station
Digital Twin Lab Activity

Select ST‑04 Quality and run all four scenarios (Vision Camera Calibration Drift, EOL Roll‑Test Sensor Noise, HV Insulation Test Lead Contact Drift, and MES Traceability Data Gaps). Trainees trace each failure signature back to the most likely originating station using the MES trace log provided in the worksheet.

Assessment

Diagnostic worksheet + traceability exercise linking an EOL failure code to its probable upstream station.

M6

Capstone — Chronic Bottleneck Diagnosis & Response

6.5 hrs ▸
Learning Objectives
  • Apply the Six Big Losses framework (breakdowns, setup/adjustment, idling/minor stops, speed loss, startup/process defects, in‑process defects) to classify losses observed across all four stations.
  • Use 5 Why and Fishbone (Ishikawa) analysis to trace a chronic symptom to root cause.
  • Execute a structured Andon‑style response protocol for a suspected chronic (vs. sporadic) issue.
  • Propose a preventive/TPM (Total Productive Maintenance) countermeasure for a given chronic bottleneck.
Core Framework: Why "Chronic" Is the Hard Case
Sporadic loss
Sudden, large deviation from normal. Line stops, alarm fires, cause is usually obvious and technician response is immediate and well‑rehearsed. Easy to see, harder to prevent recurrence without root‑cause follow‑up.
Chronic loss
Small, recurring, often within "normal variation" tolerance — a few seconds of added cycle time, a slightly elevated reject rate. No alarm fires. Accumulates into major OEE loss over a shift. Requires trend data, not alarms, to detect.
Diagnostic Toolkit Taught in This Module
  1. OEE trend monitoring — reading the digital twin's cycle‑time and reject‑rate history rather than just the current‑instant value.
  2. Pareto of micro‑stops — ranking small, frequent stoppages by cumulative time lost, not by individual severity.
  3. 5 Why — a five‑iteration questioning technique to move from symptom to actionable root cause.
  4. Fishbone / Ishikawa — categorizing candidate causes under Machine, Method, Material, Man, Measurement, Environment.
  5. Andon response protocol — when to call it, when to let the line run and log it, and how to escalate a suspected chronic issue for engineering follow‑up.
Digital Twin Capstone Lab

Run the Hidden‑Chronic Cascade Demo on the Simulator tab. A torque‑tool air‑pressure drift at Station 3 is introduced sub‑threshold — the line keeps running and no alarm fires at Station 3. Trainees must:

  1. Notice the drift using the OEE/cycle‑time trend, not an alarm.
  2. Trace the downstream EOL failure signature at Station 4 back to Station 3 using the MES trace log.
  3. Build a 5 Why chain and a Fishbone diagram for the root cause.
  4. Draft a corrective action and a preventive TPM countermeasure (e.g., scheduled air‑pressure/bit‑wear checks, statistical process control limits on torque).
Assessment

Capstone diagnostic report (5 Why + Fishbone + corrective/preventive action) presented to the class; instructor rubric provided in the Instructor Guide tab.

§2

Materials & Setup Checklist
  • Laptop or tablet per pair, modern browser (Chrome/Edge/Safari), no install required — this HTML file runs standalone.
  • Projector/large display for whole‑class walkthroughs of Modules 1 and 6.
  • Printed or digital trainee logsheet for baseline KPI recording (M1) and diagnostic worksheets (M2–M5).
  • Optional physical props: worn vs. new weld electrode tip, spray nozzle sample, torque wrench with pressure gauge — significantly improves retention when paired with the digital twin scenario.
  • Whiteboard or flip chart for live 5 Why / Fishbone construction in Module 6.
§3

Common Trainee Misconceptions
"If the line didn't stop, nothing is wrong."
Directly address this before Module 6. Chronic losses are defined by their invisibility to alarm systems — this is the single most important reframe in the program.
"A robot fault always means a broken part."
Many chronic issues (TCP drift, calibration drift, pressure drop) are configuration or consumable‑wear issues, not part failures. This distinction changes the correct response (recalibrate/replace consumable vs. full maintenance ticket).
"EV lines don't need this — they're mostly robots."
Reinforce the program's core premise explicitly: automation changes who does the diagnosis, not whether diagnosis is needed. A fully robotic station still drifts, wears, and needs a technician who can read its data.
§4

Simulator Scenario Answer Key

Full explanations trainees see on screen after answering are reproduced here for quick instructor reference during debrief.

Station 1 — Body Assembly
ScenarioCorrect Root CauseCorrective ActionPreventive / TPM
Electrode Tip WearProgressive electrode mushrooming raises contact resistance, weakening weld nuggets over hundreds of cycles.Dress or replace electrode tip per wear schedule; verify weld current/pressure setpoints.Time‑ or count‑based tip dressing interval; nugget‑size SPC trending.
TCP DriftMinor unlogged collision or servo backlash shifted the robot's tool‑center‑point reference.Re‑teach/re‑calibrate TCP; inspect gun mount for looseness.Post‑collision auto‑flag and mandatory re‑cal step before resuming production.
Station 2 — Paint
ScenarioCorrect Root CauseCorrective ActionPreventive / TPM
Spray Nozzle Partial ClogPartial dried‑paint blockage narrows spray pattern, causing uneven film build.Purge/clean nozzle per SOP; verify flow rate against spec.Scheduled nozzle purge cycle; flow‑rate monitoring with low‑flow alert threshold.
Booth Humidity DriftHVAC drift outside cure window affects adhesion and gloss consistency.Recalibrate booth climate control; hold suspect units for inspection.Continuous humidity/temperature logging with trend‑based (not just threshold) alerting.
Station 3 — General Assembly
ScenarioCorrect Root CauseCorrective ActionPreventive / TPM
Torque Tool Air Pressure DropGradual supply‑pressure decay reduces delivered torque below spec without tripping a hard fault.Restore line pressure; re‑torque affected fasteners; verify with calibrated tool.In‑line pressure sensor with SPC control limits, not just min/max cutoff.
Battery Pack Fastener Feeder JamFeeder track misfeed intermittently starves the tool of fasteners.Clear jam; inspect feeder rail and fastener batch quality.Feeder vibration/jam sensor with count‑based preventive service interval.
Station 4 — Quality
ScenarioCorrect Root CauseCorrective ActionPreventive / TPM
Vision Camera Calibration DriftLighting or lens calibration shifted, changing the false‑reject/false‑accept threshold.Recalibrate camera against reference target; re‑inspect held units.Scheduled calibration checks; environmental lighting monitoring.
EOL Roll‑Test Sensor NoiseSensor signal noise causes intermittent false‑fail readings, inflating retest loops.Inspect sensor wiring/shielding; replace if noise persists after reseating connections.Signal quality trend monitoring flags noise before it causes false fails.
Hidden‑Chronic Cascade Demo

The scripted scenario introduces a sub‑threshold torque drift at Station 3 that does not trigger a Station 3 alarm, but produces an intermittent functional‑test failure at Station 4. Correct trainee reasoning: the EOL failure code should be traced via the MES build record back to the Station 3 fastening operation, not treated as a Station 4 equipment problem. This is the single learning moment the whole capstone is built around — spend extra debrief time here.

§5

Capstone Assessment Rubric (M6)
CriterionWeightMeets Standard
Correct detection method (trend, not alarm)20%Trainee explicitly identifies the issue via OEE/cycle‑time trend rather than waiting for an alarm.
Correct upstream trace20%Trainee correctly links the Station 4 failure signature to the Station 3 origin using the MES trace log.
5 Why chain quality20%Five coherent iterations reaching an actionable, not superficial, root cause.
Fishbone completeness15%Candidate causes populate at least 4 of the 6 categories (Machine, Method, Material, Man, Measurement, Environment) before elimination.
Corrective action10%Action addresses the actual root cause, is specific, and is feasible on shift.
Preventive/TPM countermeasure15%Countermeasure prevents recurrence (e.g., SPC limit, sensor addition, PM interval) rather than repeating the corrective action.
§6

Adapting This Program
  • Non‑EV lines: Module 4 content maps directly back to a conventional engine/transmission assembly station by substituting "battery pack/e‑motor marriage" with "powertrain marriage" — the automation and diagnostic principles are unchanged.
  • Shorter delivery: Modules 1–5 can run as a 17‑hour Foundation‑only track without the capstone for a general line‑orientation audience; add Module 6 separately as a 6.5‑hour Diagnostic add‑on for maintenance/technician trainees specifically.
  • Language localization: All simulator scenario text is contained in a single JavaScript data object near the top of the script (search for SCENARIOS) to simplify translation for non‑English cohorts.
